card.summary_ko: 이규보가 『구삼국사』를 읽고 지은 장편 서사시. 해모수와 유화, 주몽의 탄생과 건국을 노래하고, 서문에서 이 신이한 이야기를 기록하는 뜻을 밝힌다. 원문에는 이규보가 단 것으로 보는 협주(분주)가 괄호 안에 함께 들어 있는데, 상당 부분이 『구삼국사』의 내용을 옮기거나 간추린 것으로 여겨진다.
card.summary_en: Yi Gyu-bo's long narrative poem written after reading the Old Samguk sa: it sings of Hae Mo-su and Yuhwa and of Jumong's birth and founding of the state, with a preface explaining why he recorded these marvels. The text includes interlinear notes (in parentheses), usually taken to be the author's own, much of which is thought to reproduce or condense the Old Samguk sa.

notes.ko:
**저자** 이규보(1168–1241, 호 백운거사)는 경기 여주(황려) 출신으로, 1170년 무신정변 이후 무신정권기에 활동한 문인이다. 과거에는 일찍 합격했으나 관직을 얻지 못한 채 지내다 최충헌이 집권한 뒤 1199년 관직에 나아갔고, 이후 최충헌·최우 정권을 섬기며 문하시랑평장사에 이르렀다. 1231년 몽골이 침입하자 강화도로 옮긴 조정에서 외교 문서를 도맡아 지었다. 유교 문인이지만 불교와 도가에도 열려 있었다. 문장으로 무신정권에 협력해 출세했다는 비판과, 시대의 모순을 시로 남겼다는 평가가 함께 있다. 문집은 『동국이상국집』이다. 〈동명왕편〉은 그가 아직 관직에 나가기 전인 26세 때 지은 시다.

**시대적 맥락** 1193년은 무신정권 초기로, 이의민이 권력을 쥐었고 경상도에서 김사미·효심의 농민 봉기가 일어나던 혼란기였다. 이규보는 『구삼국사』의 「동명왕본기」를 읽고 감동하여 고구려 시조 주몽의 건국신화를 오언 장편 서사시로 옮겼다. 서문은 김부식의 『삼국사기』(1145)가 이 신이한 이야기를 줄인 것을 아쉬워하며, 이를 허황한 이야기가 아닌 나라를 세운 신성한 사적으로 본다고 밝혔다. 『구삼국사』가 전하지 않아 이 시는 동명왕 신화의 중요한 자료가 되었다. 시는 『동국이상국집』에 실려 전하며, 고려를 고구려의 계승자로 보는 자부심의 표현으로도 읽힌다.

**배경 / Background**
이규보(李奎報, 1168–1241)가 1193년(계축년, 26세)에 지은 오언 장편 서사시로, 문집 『동국이상국집』 권3에 실려 있다. 서문에 따르면 지은이는 『구삼국사』의 「동명왕본기」를 읽고 감동하여 이 시를 썼다. 『구삼국사』는 오늘날 전하지 않는다. 이 원문은 서문과 시 전체(이 판본에서 280행; 그중 한 행은 15자로 되어 있어 오언 282구에 해당)를 담고 있으며, 시 속 협주(分註)가 괄호 안에 함께 들어 있다. 협주는 통상 이규보 자신이 단 주석으로 보며, 상당 부분이 지금은 전하지 않는 『구삼국사』 「동명왕본기」의 내용을 옮기거나 간추린 것으로 여겨진다(예: 해부루·금와 이야기, 하백과의 변신 겨루기, 송양과의 활쏘기, 유리의 부러진 칼 이야기). 다만 『구삼국사』가 전하지 않아 어디까지가 원문 그대로의 인용이고 어디부터 이규보의 요약·설명인지는 확인할 수 없으며, 글자 풀이(例 輢, 叶韻)나 『통전』 인용 같은 짧은 주도 섞여 있다. 번역은 AI가 한 것으로, 불확실한 부분은 [?]로 표시했다.

**의의 / Significance**
고구려 시조 동명왕(주몽)의 건국신화를 자세히 전하는 현존 자료이자, 한국 한문학에서 가장 이른 장편 서사시의 하나로 평가된다. 서문은 이 신이한 이야기를 허황된 것이 아니라 '나라를 세운 신령한 자취'로 보며, 우리나라가 '성인의 도읍'이라는 자부심을 밝힌다.

**형식과 주제 / Form and themes**
오언고시(五言古詩) 한 구 다섯 글자로 이어지며 두 구가 한 쌍을 이룬다. 해모수와 유화의 만남, 주몽의 탄생·시련·남행, 비류왕 송양과의 대결을 순서대로 서술하고, 끝에서 유방·광무제의 탄생 설화를 들어 건국 시조의 신성함을 거듭 말한 뒤 수성(守成)의 군주에게 경계를 남긴다.

**읽기 도움 / Reading help**
- 直筆(직필): 사실을 굽히지 않고 곧게 쓰는 붓(사관의 글쓰기).
- 神異(신이): 신령하고 이상한 일.
- 河伯(하백): 강의 신.
- 草創(초창): 나라를 처음 세움. 守成(수성): 이룬 것을 지킴.
- 不語怪力亂神: 『논어』, 공자는 괴이·힘·난·귀신을 말하지 않았다.
- 赤帝子(적제자), 赤伏符(적복부): 한 고조(적제의 아들)와 광무제(적복부 참언)의 천명을 가리키는 말.
- 서문의 '▣▣'는 원문의 판독 불가 두 글자.
- 시 중 몇몇 희귀 글자(𣳎, 𩣚, 𥈭)는 한자음을 확정하기 어려워 그대로 두었고, 趡(유), 㠑(죄), 㠥(뢰)의 음도 자전을 따른 것으로 확실하지 않다. 高帝(고제)가 누구인지, '玉指' 대목의 뜻, '我爲豺而趡'의 '我'(왕 자신의 목소리)도 확정하기 어렵다. 시의 '이억만 팔천칠백팔십 리'는 원문 그대로의 수치이다.

**번역 / Korean translation**

**서문**

세상에는 동명왕의 신이한 일을 많이들 이야기한다. 어리석은 사내와 철없는 아낙네조차 그 일을 곧잘 말한다. 나는 일찍이 이를 듣고 웃으며 말했다. "돌아가신 스승 중니(공자)께서는 괴이함·힘·어지러움·귀신을 말씀하지 않으셨다. 이는 실로 황당하고 기괴한 일이라 우리 무리가 말할 바가 아니다." 그러나 『위서』와 『통전』을 읽어 보니 그것들도 이 일을 실었다. 다만 간략하고 자세하지 않았으니, 어쩌면 안(內)은 자세히 하고 밖(外)은 간략히 한다는 뜻이 아니겠는가(중국의 일은 자세히, 외국의 일은 간략히).

계축년(1193) 4월에 『구삼국사』를 얻어 「동명왕본기」를 보니, 그 신이한 자취가 세상에서 말하는 것보다 더하였다. 그러나 이 역시 처음에는 믿을 수 없어 귀신의 환술이라 여겼다. 세 번 거듭 읽고 깊이 음미하니 점차 그 근원에 이르렀고, 환(幻)이 아니라 성(聖)이요, 귀(鬼)가 아니라 신(神)이었다. 하물며 나라의 사서는 곧은 붓으로 쓴 글인데 어찌 함부로 전했겠는가. 김공 부식이 국사를 다시 지을 때 이 일을 꽤 줄였는데, 아마 공은 국사란 세상을 바로잡는 글이니 크게 이상한 일을 후세에 보여서는 안 된다고 여겨 줄인 것일까.

살피건대 『당현종본기』와 「양귀비전」에는 모두 방사가 하늘에 오르고 땅에 들어간 일이 없다. 오직 시인 백낙천이 그 일이 사라질까 염려하여 노래를 지어 기록하였다. 저것은 실로 황음하고 기이하고 허탄한 일인데도 오히려 읊어 후세에 보였다. 하물며 동명의 일은 변화와 신이로 뭇사람의 눈을 현혹하는 것이 아니라 실로 나라를 세운 신령한 자취이니, 이를 서술하지 않으면 후세에 장차 무엇을 보겠는가. 이에 시를 지어 ▣▣(두 글자 판독 불가) 기록하여, 천하로 하여금 우리나라가 본래 성인의 도읍임을 알게 하고자 할 뿐이다.

**시 본문 (두 구씩 한 줄)**

원기가 혼돈에서 갈라지니, 천황씨와 지황씨가 나셨다.  
머리가 열셋, 머리가 열하나였다 하며, 몸과 모습이 몹시 기이하였다.  
그 밖의 성스러운 제왕들도 경서와 사서에 갖추어 실려 있다.  
여절은 큰 별에 감응하여 대호(大昊) 지(摯)를 낳았고,  
여추는 전욱을 낳았으니, 역시 요광성의 빛에 감응한 것이다.  
복희는 희생(犧牲)을 마련하였고, 수인은 처음으로 나무를 비벼 불을 일으켰다.  
명협이 돋음은 고제(高帝)의 상서요, 곡식이 비처럼 내림은 신농의 상서였다.  
푸른 하늘은 여와가 기웠고, 홍수는 대우가 다스렸다.  
황제가 장차 승천하려 할 때, 수염 늘어진 용이 스스로 이르렀다.  
태고의 순박한 시절에는 신령하고 성스러운 일을 다 적기 어렵다.  
후세는 점점 야박해지고, 풍속은 으레 사치로 흘렀다.  
성인이 간혹 나시더라도 신령한 자취는 보이는 일이 드물다.  
한나라 신작 3년 초여름, 북두의 자루가 사(巳)방에 설 때,  
해동의 해모수는 참으로 하늘의 아들이었다.  
처음 허공에서 내려올 때 몸은 다섯 용의 수레를 탔고,  
따르는 자 백여 명은 고니를 타고 깃옷을 나부꼈다.  
맑은 음악은 낭랑히 울리고, 채색 구름은 하늘하늘 떠올랐다.  
예로부터 천명을 받은 임금이 어찌 하늘이 내리지 않은 이가 있었겠는가마는,  
대낮에 푸른 하늘에서 내려옴은 예전에 본 적이 없는 일이다.  
아침엔 인간 세상에 머물고, 저녁엔 하늘 궁궐로 돌아갔다.  
내가 옛사람에게 듣기로, 푸른 하늘은 땅에서 이억만 팔천칠백팔십 리(엄청난 거리)라 한다.  
사다리와 잔도로는 오르기 어렵고, 날개로 날면 쉬이 지친다.  
그런데 아침저녁으로 제멋대로 오르내림은, 이 이치가 또 어찌 된 일인가.  
성 북쪽에 청하(靑河)가 있어, 하백의 세 딸이 아름다웠다.  
오리 머리빛 물결을 가르고 나와, 웅심의 물가로 놀러 갔다.  
쟁그랑 패옥이 울리고, 날씬한 얼굴은 꽃처럼 고왔다.  
처음엔 한고의 물가인가 의심하였고, 다시 낙수의 모래톱인가 생각하였다.  
왕이 사냥을 나갔다가 보고, 눈으로 좇으며 자못 마음을 두었으니,  
이는 화려한 빛깔을 좋아해서가 아니라, 참으로 후사 잇기가 급해서였다.  
세 딸이 임금이 오는 것을 보고, 물에 들어가 서로 피하였다.  
궁전을 지어 놓고, 그들이 함께 와 노닐기를 몰래 기다리려 하여,  
말채찍으로 땅에 한 번 금을 그으니, 구리 집이 문득 우뚝 섰다.  
비단 자리를 깔아 찬란히 빛나고, 금 술동이에 진한 맛난 술을 놓았다.  
사뿐사뿐 과연 스스로 들어와, 마주 앉아 마시더니 곧 취하였다.  
왕이 때맞춰 나와 길을 막으니, 놀라 달아나다 하마터면 넘어질 뻔하였다.  
맏딸은 이름이 유화인데, 왕에게 붙잡힌 이가 바로 그이다.  
하백이 크게 노하여, 사자를 급하고 빠르게 보내,  
이르기를 "너는 누구이기에, 감히 이리 가볍고 방자하게 구느냐" 하였다.  
대답하기를 "나는 천제의 아들이니, 높은 가문으로서 혼인을 청한다" 하고,  
하늘을 가리키니 용이 끄는 수레가 내려와, 곧바로 깊은 바다 궁에 이르렀다.  
하백이 이에 왕에게 말하기를 "혼인은 큰일이라,  
중매와 폐백에 통하는 법이 있거늘, 어찌 제멋대로 하는가.  
그대가 상제의 후손이라면, 신통한 변화를 시험해 보기를 청한다" 하였다.  
잔물결 이는 푸른 물결 속에서, 하백은 잉어로 변하니,  
왕은 곧 수달로 변하여, 반 걸음도 기다리지 않고 즉시 잡았다.  
또 두 날개가 돋아나 훨훨 꿩으로 변하니,  
왕은 또 신령한 매로 변하여, 덮쳐 치는 것이 어찌나 사나운지.  
저는 사슴이 되어 달아나고, 나는 승냥이가 되어 쫓았다.  
하백은 신통함이 있음을 알고, 술상을 차려 서로 잔치하며 기뻐하였다.  
취하기를 기다려 가죽 수레에 싣고, 딸을 수레 난간 곁에 함께 두어,  
그 딸과 함께 하늘 위로 고삐를 나란히 오르게 할 생각이었다.  
그 수레가 물을 채 나서기 전에, 술이 깨어 홀연 놀라 일어나,  
여인의 황금 비녀를 뽑아 가죽을 찔러 구멍으로 빠져나가,  
홀로 붉은 하늘로 올라가, 쓸쓸히 말머리를 돌리지 않았다.  
하백이 딸을 꾸짖어 입술을 잡아당기니 석 자나 늘어졌다.  
이에 우발수로 귀양 보내, 오직 시종 둘(여종과 사내종)만 딸려 보냈다.  
어부가 물결 속을 보다가, 기이한 짐승이 어슬렁어슬렁 다님을 보고,  
금와왕에게 아뢰니, 쇠그물을 철철 흐르는 물에 던졌다.  
바위에 앉은 여인을 끌어올리니, 모습이 몹시 두려울 만하였다.  
입술이 길어 말을 못 하다가, 세 번 자르고서야 이를 드러내었다.  
왕은 모수의 아내임을 알고, 이에 별궁에 두었다.  
햇빛을 품고 주몽을 낳으니, 이해는 계(癸)년이었다.  
골상은 참으로 가장 기이하였고, 울음소리 또한 매우 웅장하였다.  
처음 태어날 때 알이 한 되만 하여, 보는 이가 모두 놀라 떨었다.  
왕이 상서롭지 못하다 여겨 "이것이 어찌 사람의 부류이겠느냐" 하고,  
마구간에 두니 뭇 말이 모두 밟지 않았고,  
깊은 산에 버리니 온갖 짐승이 모두 에워싸 지켰다.  
어머니가 마침내 거두어 기르니, 한 달이 지나 말을 하기 시작하였다.  
스스로 말하기를 "파리가 눈을 물어, 누워도 편히 잘 수 없습니다" 하니,  
어머니가 활과 화살을 만들어 주었는데, 그 활은 헛되이 당기는 법이 없었다.  
나이가 차츰 자라나, 재주와 능력이 날로 갖추어졌다.  
부여왕의 태자가 마음속으로 시기하여,  
말하기를 "주몽이란 자는 반드시 범상한 사내가 아니니,  
일찍 도모하지 않으면 그 근심은 참으로 끝이 없으리라" 하였다.  
왕이 가서 말을 기르게 하니, 그 뜻을 시험하려 함이었다.  
스스로 생각하되 "나는 하늘의 손자로서 마소 치는 천역을 하다니 참으로 부끄럽다" 하고,  
가슴을 어루만지며 늘 몰래 말하기를 "내 삶은 죽느니만 못하다" 하였다.  
남쪽 땅으로 가서 나라를 세우고 성읍을 세울 생각이었으나,  
자애로운 어머니가 계시기에 이별이 참으로 쉽지 않았다.  
어머니가 이 말을 듣고 맑은 눈물을 흘리며 닦고서,  
"너는 부디 걱정하지 마라. 나 또한 늘 가슴 아파했다.  
선비가 먼 길을 가려면 반드시 준마에 의지해야 한다" 하였다.  
함께 마구간에 가서 곧 긴 채찍으로 때리니,  
뭇 말이 모두 뛰어 달아나는데, 한 마리 붉은 말은 빛깔이 고왔다.  
두 길 울타리를 뛰어넘으니, 비로소 준마임을 알았다.  
몰래 바늘로 혀를 찔러 두니, 시고 아파 먹이를 받지 않아,  
며칠 안 되어 몸이 몹시 야위어, 도리어 둔한 말과 같아졌다.  
그 뒤 왕이 둘러보다가 말을 내어 주었는데, 바로 이 말이었다.  
얻고서 비로소 바늘을 뽑고, 밤낮으로 자주 먹이를 더해 주었다.  
몰래 어진 벗 셋을 맺으니, 이 사람들은 모두 지혜가 많았다.  
남쪽으로 가서 엄체에 이르렀으나, 건너려 해도 댈 배가 없었다.  
채찍을 쥐고 저 푸른 하늘을 가리키며, 개연히 길게 탄식하여 말하기를,  
"천제의 손자이자 하백의 외손이, 난을 피해 이곳에 이르렀습니다.  
가련한 외로운 아들의 마음을, 천지가 차마 버리시겠습니까" 하고,  
활을 들어 강물을 치자, 물고기와 자라가 머리와 꼬리를 나란히 하여,  
우뚝 다리를 이루니, 비로소 건널 수 있었다.  
이윽고 추격병이 이르러, 다리에 오르자 다리는 곧 무너졌다.  
비둘기 한 쌍이 보리를 물고 날아와, 신모(神母)의 사자가 되었다.  
지세 좋은 곳에 왕도를 열었는데, 산천은 울창하고 우뚝하였다.  
스스로 풀 자리 위에 앉아, 군신의 자리를 대략 정하였다.  
아, 비류왕이여, 어찌 제 분수를 헤아리지 못하는가.  
신선의 후손임을 몹시 자랑하며, 제왕 손자의 귀함을 알아보지 못하고,  
한갓 부용국으로 삼으려 하니, 내놓는 말이 삼가지도 두려워하지도 않았다.  
그림 속 사슴의 배꼽을 맞히지 못하는데, 나는 옥가락지를 쓰러뜨려 그를 놀라게 하였다.  
와서 북과 뿔피리가 달라진 것을 보고는 감히 제 것이라 하지 못하였고,  
와서 집 기둥이 낡은 것을 보고는 혀를 내두르며 도리어 부끄러워하였다.  
동명이 서쪽으로 사냥 갔을 때, 우연히 눈빛 흰 사슴을 잡아,  
해원 위에 거꾸로 매달고, 감히 스스로 저주하여 말하기를,  
"하늘이 비류에 비를 내려, 그 도읍과 변방을 떠내려가게 잠기게 하지 않으면,  
내 진실로 너를 놓아주지 않으리니, 너는 내 분노를 도우라" 하였다.  
사슴의 울음소리가 몹시 애처로워, 위로 하늘의 귀에 사무쳤다.  
장맛비가 이레를 쏟아져, 회수와 사수를 기울인 듯 퍼부었다.  
송양이 몹시 근심하고 두려워, 물길을 따라 부질없이 갈대를 가로질렀으나,  
백성들이 다투어 와서 매달리며, 땀을 흘리고 서로 노려보았다.  
동명이 곧 채찍으로, 물에 금을 그으니 끓어오르던 물이 멈추었다.  
송양이 온 나라를 들어 항복하니, 이후로 아무도 나를 헐뜯지 못하였다.  
검은 구름이 골령을 덮어, 구불구불한 산이 보이지 않더니,  
사람 수천 명이 있는 듯, 나무 찍는 소리가 어슴푸레 들렸다.  
왕이 이르기를 "하늘이 나를 위해, 그 기슭에 성을 쌓게 하시는구나" 하였는데,  
홀연 구름과 안개가 걷히자, 궁궐이 높이 우뚝 솟아 있었다.  
재위 십구 년에, 하늘에 올라 다시 내려와 다스리지 않았다.  
호방하고 기이한 절개가 있었다. 맏아들은 유리라 하니,  
칼을 얻어 아버지의 자리를 이었고, 물동이 구멍을 막아 사람의 꾸짖음을 그치게 했다.  
나는 천성이 본래 질박하여, 기이하고 괴이한 것을 좋아하지 않는다.  
처음 동명의 일을 보고는, 환상인가 귀신인가 의심하였으나,  
천천히 차츰 깊이 들어가 보니, 그 변화는 헤아려 논하기 어려웠다.  
하물며 곧은 붓으로 쓴 글이라, 한 글자도 헛된 글자가 없음에랴.  
신령하고도 신령하도다, 만세에 옳다 할 바로다.  
이로 인해 나라를 연 임금을 생각하니, 성인이 아니고서야 어찌 되겠는가.  
유온(劉媼)이 큰 못가에서 쉬다가, 꿈속에서 신을 만났는데,  
우레와 번개가 어둠을 메우고, 교룡이 괴이하게 서려 있었다.  
이로 인해 곧 잉태하여, 성인 유계(劉季)를 낳았다.  
이는 곧 적제의 아들이니, 그 흥함에 특별한 복이 많았다.  
세조(世祖)가 처음 태어났을 때, 방 안 가득 빛이 환하게 빛났고,  
스스로 적복부에 응하여, 황건의 거짓을 쓸어 없앴다.  
예로부터 제왕이 일어날 때, 상서로운 징조가 어지러이 무성하였으나,  
뒤를 이은 자는 대개 게으르고 거칠어, 함께 선왕의 제사를 끊었다.  
이에 알겠노라, 수성(守成)하는 임금은 '여뀌에 모인다'는 경계와 '작은 일을 삼가라'는 말을 새기고,  
너그러움과 어짊으로 자리를 지키며, 예와 의로 백성을 교화하여,  
길이길이 자손에게 전하고, 나라를 다스림이 여러 해에 이르러야 함을.
notes.en:
**About the author** Yi Gyu-bo (1168-1241, pen name Baegun geosa) came from Yeoju (Hwangnyeo) in Gyeonggi and was a literatus active under the military regime that followed the 1170 military coup. He passed the examinations early but had no office until 1199, after Choe Chung-heon came to power; he then served the Choe Chung-heon and Choe U regimes and rose to senior minister. When the Mongols invaded in 1231 he wrote most of the diplomatic correspondence for the court that had moved to Ganghwa Island. A Confucian literatus open to Buddhism and Daoism, he is criticised for rising by serving the military regime with his pen, and praised for recording his age's contradictions in verse. His collected works are the Dongguk Isanggukjip. The Epic of King Dongmyeong was written at 26, before he held any office.

**Historical context** 1193 was early in the military regime, when Yi Ui-min held power and peasant uprisings such as Gim Sa-mi and Hyo-sim's broke out in Gyeongsang; it was a turbulent time. After reading the 'Annals of King Dongmyeong' in the old Samguksa (Gu Samguksa), Yi Gyu-bo turned the foundation myth of Jumong, founder of Goguryeo, into a long five-syllable narrative poem. His preface regrets that Kim Bu-sik's Samguksagi (1145) shortened this marvellous story and says he regards it not as fantasy but as a sacred record of a state's founding. Because the Gu Samguksa is lost, the poem is a key source for the myth. It survives in the Dongguk Isanggukjip and is also read as an expression of pride in Goryeo as heir to Goguryeo.

**Background**
A long five-character narrative poem composed by Yi Gyu-bo (1168–1241) in 1193 (the gyechuk year, when he was 26), included in volume 3 of his collected works, Dongguk Isangguk jip. According to the preface, he wrote it after reading the Basic Annals of King Dongmyeong in the Old Samguk sa, which no longer survives. This text contains the preface and the whole poem (280 lines in this edition, one of which is a 15-character line, i.e. 282 five-character lines), with the author's own interlinear notes (分註) kept in parentheses at their places in the poem. These notes are usually taken to be Yi Gyu-bo's own commentary, and a large part of them is thought to reproduce or condense the Basic Annals in the lost Old Samguk sa (for example the Haeburu and Geumwa story, the shape-shifting contest with the River Count, the archery contest with Songyang, and Yuri's broken sword). Since that text is lost, it cannot be checked where a note is a verbatim quotation and where it is Yi's summary or explanation, and some notes are only short glosses (e.g. 輢, 叶韻) or a quotation of the Tongdian. They are translated literally by AI, with doubtful readings marked [?].

**Significance**
It is a detailed surviving account of the founding myth of Goguryeo's progenitor Dongmyeong (Jumong), and is regarded as one of the earliest long narrative poems in Korean Literary Chinese. The preface treats the marvels not as absurd but as "divine traces of founding a nation," and asserts pride that Korea was originally "the capital of a sage."

**Form and themes**
Five-character ancient-style verse, with lines in couplets. It narrates the meeting of Hae Mo-su and Yuhwa, Jumong's birth, trials and journey south, and his contest with King Songyang of Biryu; it closes by citing the birth tales of Liu Bang and Emperor Guangwu to affirm the sacredness of founders, then addresses a warning to rulers who merely preserve what was won.

**Reading help**
- 直筆 (jikpil): the "straight brush", a historian's unbending record.
- 神異 (sini): marvellous, divine and strange.
- 河伯 (Habaek): the River Count, god of the river.
- 草創 (chochang) founding; 守成 (suseong) preserving what has been achieved.
- 不語怪力亂神: from the Analects, Confucius did not speak of prodigies, force, disorder or spirits.
- 赤帝子, 赤伏符: the Red Emperor's son (Liu Bang); the Chifu ("Red Fu") prophecy talisman (Emperor Guangwu); omens of the Han founders.
- "▣▣" in the preface marks two illegible characters in the source.
- A few rare characters in the poem (𣳎, 𩣚, 𥈭) have uncertain readings and are left as written in the reading line; the readings given for 趡 (yu), 㠑 (joe) and 㠥 (roe) follow reference tables and are not firmly verified. Also uncertain: who "Gaodi" (高帝) is, the sense of the "jade ring" (玉指) episode, and the "I" in "I became a dhole" (the king speaking in his own voice). The distance "二億萬八千七百八十 li" is given as written.

**Korean translation / 번역**
See the Korean-language notes above for the full Korean rendering of the preface and poem.

paragraphs.orig: 世多說東明王神異之事。雖愚夫騃婦。亦頗能說其事。僕嘗聞之。笑曰。先師仲尼。不語怪力亂神。此實荒唐奇詭之事。非吾曹所說。及讀魏書通典。亦載其事。然略而未詳。豈詳內略外之意耶。越癸丑四月。得舊三國史。見東明王本紀。其神異之迹。踰世之所說者。然亦初不能信之。意以爲鬼幻。及三復耽味。漸涉其源。非幻也。乃聖也。非鬼也。乃神也。況國史直筆之書。豈妄傳之哉。金公富軾重撰國史。頗略其事。意者公以爲國史矯世之書。不可以大異之事爲示於後世而略之耶。按唐玄宗本紀。楊貴妃傳。並無方士升天入地之事。唯詩人白樂天恐其事淪沒。作歌以志之。彼實荒淫奇誕之事。猶且詠之。以示于後。矧東明之事。非以變化神異眩惑衆目。乃實創國之神迹。則此而不述。後將何觀。是用作詩以▣▣記之。欲使夫天下知我國本聖人之都耳。

paragraphs.en:
Many in the world tell of the marvellous deeds of King Dongmyeong. Even foolish men and simple women can tell the story quite well. I once heard it and laughed, saying, "The late Master Zhongni [Confucius] did not speak of prodigies, force, disorder or spirits. This is truly absurd and bizarre, not a matter for people like us to talk about." But when I read the Wei shu and the Tongdian, they too recorded the matter, though briefly and without detail; perhaps this reflects the principle of being detailed about what is within and brief about what is outside [i.e. detailed about China, brief about foreign lands]?

In the fourth month of the gyechuk year [1193] I obtained the Old Samguk sa and read the Basic Annals of King Dongmyeong. Its marvellous traces exceeded what the world tells. Even so, at first I could not believe it, and took it to be a ghostly illusion. But after reading it three times and savouring it, I gradually waded to its source, and it was not illusion but sacred, not ghostly but divine. How much more so, since a national history is a book of straight brush: how could it hand down falsehoods? When Duke Kim Bu-sik revised the national history, he considerably abridged this matter. Perhaps the Duke took the national history to be a book that corrects the age, and thought that extraordinary matters should not be shown to later generations, and so abridged it?

I note that in the Basic Annals of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang and the Biography of Yang Guifei there is nothing of the magician ascending to heaven and entering the earth; only the poet Bai Letian, fearing that the story would be lost, composed a song to record it. That was a truly licentious, fantastic and extravagant matter, and he still sang of it to show posterity. How much more, then, the matter of Dongmyeong, which does not dazzle and bewilder the eyes of the multitude with transformations and marvels but is truly the divine trace of the founding of a nation. If we do not narrate this, what will later ages have to look to? For this reason I have made a poem to [two illegible characters] record it, wishing to let the world know that our country was originally the capital of a sage.

元氣判𣳎渾。天皇地皇氏。十三十一頭。體貌多奇異。其餘聖帝王。亦備載經史。女節感大星。乃生大昊摯。女樞生顓頊。亦感瑤光暐。伏羲制牲犧。燧人始鑽燧。生蓂高帝祥。雨粟神農瑞。靑天女媧補。洪水大禹理。黃帝將升天。胡髥龍自至。太古淳朴時。靈聖難備記。後世漸澆漓。風俗例汰侈。聖人間或生。神迹少所示。漢神雀三年。孟夏斗立巳。(漢神雀三年四月甲寅。)海東解慕漱。眞是天之子。(本記云。夫余王解夫婁老無子。祭山川求嗣。所御馬至鯤淵。見大石流淚。王怪之。使人轉其石。有小兒金色蛙形。王曰。此天錫我令胤乎。乃收養之。名曰金蛙。立爲太子。其相阿蘭弗曰。日者天降我曰。將使吾子孫。立國於此。汝其避之。東海之濱有地。號迦葉原。土宜五穀。可都也。阿蘭弗勸王移都。號東夫余。於舊都。解慕漱爲天帝子來都。)初從空中下。身乘五龍軌。從者百餘人。騎鵠紛襂襹。淸樂動鏘洋。彩雲浮旖旎。(漢神雀三年壬戌歲。天帝遣太子降遊扶余王古都。號解慕漱。從天而下。乘五龍車。從者百餘人。皆騎白鵠。彩雲浮於上。音樂動雲中。止熊心山。經十餘日始下。首戴烏羽之冠。腰帶龍光之劒。)自古受命君。何是非天賜。白日下靑冥。從昔所未視。朝居人世中。暮反天宮裡。(朝則聽事。暮卽升天。世謂之天王郞。)吾聞於古人。蒼穹之去地二億萬八千七百八十里。梯棧躡難升。羽翮飛易瘁。朝夕恣升降。此理復何爾。城北有靑河。(靑河今鴨綠江也。)河伯三女美。(長曰柳花。次曰萱花。季曰葦花。)擘出鴨頭波。往遊熊心涘。(自靑河出遊熊心淵上。)鏘琅佩玉鳴。綽約顔花媚。(神姿艶麗。雜佩鏘洋。與漢皐無異。)初疑漢皐濱。復想洛水沚。王因出獵見。目送頗留意。玆非悅紛華。誠急生繼嗣。(王謂左右曰。得而爲妃。可有後胤。)三女見君來。入水尋相避。擬將作宮殿。潛候同來戱。馬撾一畫地。銅室欻然峙。錦席鋪絢明。金罇置淳旨。蹁躚果自入。對酌還徑醉。(其女見王卽入水。左右曰。大王何不作宮殿。俟女入室。當戶遮之。王以爲然。以馬鞭畫地。銅室俄成壯麗。於室中。設三席置樽酒。其女各坐其席。相勸飮酒大醉云云。)王時出橫遮。驚走僅顚躓。(王俟三女大醉急出。遮女等驚走。長女柳花。爲王所止。)長女曰柳花。是爲王所止。河伯大怒嗔。遣使急且駛。告云渠何人。乃敢放輕肆。報云天帝子。高族請相累。指天降龍馭。徑到海宮邃。(河伯大怒。遣使告曰。汝是何人。留我女乎。王報云。我是天帝之子。今欲與河伯結婚。河伯又使告曰。汝若天帝之子。於我有求昏者。當使媒云云。今輒留我女。何其失禮。王慙之。將往見河伯。不能入室。欲放其女。女旣與王定情。不肯離去。乃勸王曰。如有龍車。可到河伯之國。王指天而告。俄而五龍車從空而下。王與女乘車。風雲忽起。至其宮。)河伯乃謂王。婚姻是大事。媒贄有通法。胡奈得自恣。(河伯備禮迎之。坐定。謂曰。婚姻之道。天下之通規。何爲失禮。辱我門宗云云。)君是上帝胤。神變請可試。漣漪碧波中。河伯化作鯉。王尋變爲獺。立捕不待跬。又復生兩翼。翩然化爲雉。王又化神鷹。摶擊何大鷙。彼爲鹿而走。我爲豺而趡。河伯知有神。置酒相燕喜。伺醉載革輿。幷置女於輢。(車傍曰輢。)意令與其女。天上同騰轡。其車未出水。酒醒忽驚起。(河伯之酒。七日乃醒。)取女黃金釵。刺革從竅出(叶韻)。獨乘赤霄上。寂寞不廻騎。(河伯曰。王是天帝之子。有何神異。王曰。唯在所試。於是。河伯於庭前水。化爲鯉。隨浪而游。王化爲獺而捕之。河伯又化爲鹿而走。王化爲豺逐之。河伯化爲雉。王化爲鷹擊之。河伯以爲誠是天帝之子。以禮成婚。恐王無將女之心。張樂置酒。勸王大醉。與女入於小革輿中。載以龍車。欲令升天。其車未出水。王卽酒醒。取女黃金釵刺革輿。從孔獨出升天。)河伯責厥女。挽吻三尺弛。乃貶優渤中。唯與婢僕二。(河伯大怒。其女曰。汝不從我訓。終欲我門。令左右絞挽女口。其唇吻長三尺。唯與奴婢二人。貶於優渤水中。優渤澤名。今在太伯山南。)漁師觀波中。奇獸行𩣚騃。乃告王金蛙。鐵網投湀湀。引得坐石女。姿貌甚堪畏。唇長不能言。三截乃啓齒。(漁師強力扶鄒告曰。近有盜梁中魚而將去者。未知何獸也。王乃使魚師以網引之。其網破裂。更造鐵網引之。始得一女。坐石而出。其女唇長不能言。令三截其唇乃言。)王知慕漱妃。仍以別宮置。懷日生朱蒙。是歲歲在癸。骨表諒最奇。啼聲亦甚偉。初生卵如升。觀者皆驚悸。王以爲不祥。此豈人之類。置之馬牧中。群馬皆不履。棄之深山中。百獸皆擁衛。(王知天帝子妃。以別宮置之。其女懷中日曜。因以有娠。神雀四年癸亥歲夏四月。生朱蒙。啼聲甚偉。骨表英奇。初生左腋生一卵。大如五升許。王怪之曰。人生鳥卵。可爲不祥。使人置之馬牧。群馬不踐。棄於深山。百獸皆護。雲陰之日。卵上恒有日光。王取卵送母養之。卵終乃開得一男。生未經月。言語竝實。)母姑擧而養。經月言語始。自言蠅噆目。臥不能安睡。母爲作弓矢。其弓不虛掎。(謂母曰。群蠅噆目。不能睡。母爲我作弓矢。其母以蓽作弓矢與之。自射紡車上蠅。發矢卽中。扶余謂善射曰朱蒙。)年至漸長大。才能日漸備。扶余王太子。其心生妬忌。乃言朱蒙者。此必非常士。若不早自圖。其患誠未已。(年至長大。才能竝備。金蛙有子七人。常共朱蒙遊獵。王子及從者四十餘人。唯獲一鹿。朱蒙射鹿至多。王子妬之。乃執朱蒙縛樹。奪鹿而去。朱蒙拔樹而去。太子帶素言於王曰。朱蒙者。神勇之士。瞻視非常。若不早圖。必有後患。)王令往牧馬。欲以試厥志。自思天之孫。廝牧良可恥。捫心常竊導。吾生不如死。意將往南土。立國立城市。爲緣慈母在。離別誠未易。(王使朱蒙牧馬。欲試其意。朱蒙內自懷恨。謂母曰。我是天帝之孫。爲人牧馬。生不如死。欲往南土造國家。母在不敢自專。其母云云。)其母聞此言。潸然抆淸淚。汝幸勿爲念。我亦常痛痞。士之涉長途。須必憑騄駬。相將往馬閑。卽以長鞭捶。群馬皆突走。一馬騂色斐。跳過二丈欄。始覺是駿驥。(通典云。朱蒙所乘。皆果下也。)潛以針刺舌。酸痛不受飼。不日形甚癯。却與駑駘似。爾後王巡觀。予馬此卽是。得之始抽針。日夜屢加餧。(其母曰。此吾之所以日夜腐心也。吾聞士之涉長途者。須憑駿足。吾能擇馬矣。遂往馬牧。卽以長鞭亂捶。群馬皆驚走。一騂馬跳過二丈之欄。朱蒙知馬駿逸。潛以針捶馬舌根。其馬舌痛。不食水草。甚瘦悴。王巡行馬牧。見群馬悉肥大喜。仍以瘦錫朱蒙。朱蒙得之。拔其針加餧云。)暗結三賢友。其人共多智。(烏伊，摩離，陜父等三人。)南行至淹滯。(一名蓋斯水。在今鴨綠東北。)欲渡無舟艤。(欲渡無舟。恐追兵奄及。迺以策指天。慨然嘆曰。我天帝之孫。河伯之甥。今避難至此。皇天后土。憐我孤子。速致舟橋。言訖。以弓打水。魚鼈浮出成橋。朱蒙乃得渡。良久追兵至。)秉策指彼蒼。慨然發長喟。天孫河伯甥。避難至於此。哀哀孤子心。天地其忍棄。操弓打河水。魚鼈騈首尾。屹然成橋梯。始乃得渡矣。俄爾追兵至。上橋橋旋圮。(追兵至河。魚鼈橋卽滅。已上橋者。皆沒死。)雙鳩含麥飛。來作神母使。(朱蒙臨別。不忍暌違。其母曰。汝勿以一母爲念。乃裹五穀種以送之。朱蒙自切生別之心。忘其麥子。朱蒙息大樹之下。有雙鳩來集。朱蒙曰。應是神母使送麥子。乃引弓射之。一矢俱擧。開喉得麥子。以水噴鳩。更蘇而飛去云云。)形勝開王都。山川鬱㠑巋。自坐茀蕝上。略定君臣位。(王自坐茀蕝之上。略定君臣之位。)咄哉沸流王。何奈不自揆。苦矜仙人後。未識帝孫貴。徒欲爲附庸。出語不愼葸。未中畫鹿臍。驚我倒玉指。(沸流王松讓出獵。見王容貌非常。引而與坐曰。僻在海隅。未曾得見君子。今日邂逅。何其幸乎。君是何人。從何而至。王曰。寡人。天帝之孫。西國之王也。敢問君王繼誰之後。讓曰。予是仙人之後。累世爲王。今地方至小。不可分爲兩王。君造國日淺。爲我附庸可乎。王曰。寡人。繼天之後。今主非神之胄。强號爲王。若不歸我。天必殛之。松讓以王累稱天孫。內自懷疑。欲試其才。乃曰願與王射矣。以畫鹿置百步內射之。其矢不入鹿臍。猶如倒手。王使人以玉指環。懸於百步之外射之。破如瓦解。松讓大驚云云。)來觀鼓角變。不敢稱我器。(王曰。以國業新造。未有鼓角威儀。沸流使者往來。我不能以王禮迎送。所以輕我也。從臣扶芬奴進曰。臣爲大王取沸流鼓角。王曰。他國藏物。汝何取乎。對曰。此天之與物。何爲不取乎。夫大王困於扶余。誰謂大王能至於此。今大王奮身於萬死之危。揚名於遼左。此天帝命而爲之。何事不成。於是扶芬奴等三人。往沸流取鼓而來。沸流王遣使告曰云云。王恐來觀鼓角。色暗如故。松讓不敢爭而去。)來觀屋柱故。咋舌還自愧。(松讓欲以立都。先後爲附庸。王造宮室。以朽木爲柱。故如千歲。松讓來見。竟不敢爭立都先後。)東明西狩時。偶獲雪色麂。(大鹿曰麂)倒懸蟹原上。敢自呪而謂。天不雨沸流。漂沒其都鄙。我固不汝放。汝可助我懫。鹿鳴聲甚哀。上徹天之耳。霖雨注七日。霈若傾淮泗。松讓甚憂懼。沿流謾橫葦。士民競來攀。流汗相𥈭眙。東明卽以鞭。畫水水停沸。松讓擧國降。是後莫予訾。(西狩獲白鹿。倒懸於蟹原。呪曰。天若不雨而漂沒沸流王都者。我固不汝放矣。欲免斯難。汝能訴天。其鹿哀鳴。聲徹于天。霖雨七日。漂沒松讓都。王以葦索橫流。乘鴨馬。百姓皆執其索。朱蒙以鞭畫水。水卽減。六月。松讓擧國來降云云。)玄雲羃鶻嶺。不見山邐迤。有人數千許。斵木聲髣髴。王曰天爲我。築城於其趾。忽然雲霧散。宮闕高㠥嵬。(七月。玄雲起鶻嶺。人不見其山。唯聞數千人聲以起土功。王曰。天爲我築城。七日。雲霧自散。城郭宮臺自然成。王拜皇天就居。)在位十九年。升天不下莅。(秋九月。王升天不下。時年四十。太子以所遺玉鞭。葬於龍山云云。)俶儻有奇節。元子曰類利。得劒繼父位。塞盆止人詈。(類利少有奇節云云。少以彈雀爲業。見一婦戴水盆。彈破之。其女怒而詈曰。無父之兒。彈破我盆。類利大慙。以泥丸彈之。塞盆孔如故。歸家問母曰。我父是誰。母以類利年少戱之曰。汝無定父。類利泣曰。人無定父。將何面目見人乎。遂欲自刎。母大驚止之曰。前言戱耳。汝父是天帝孫。河伯甥。怨爲扶餘之臣。逃往南土。始造國家。汝往見之乎。對曰。父爲人君。子爲人臣。吾雖不才。豈不愧乎。母曰。汝父去時有遺言。吾有藏物七嶺七谷石上之松。能得此者。乃我之子也。類利自往山谷。搜求不得。疲倦而還。類利聞堂柱有悲聲。其柱乃石上之松木。體有七稜。類利自解之曰。七嶺七谷者。七稜也。石上松者。柱也。起而就視之。柱上有孔。得毀劒一片。大喜。前漢鴻嘉四年夏四月。奔高句麗。以劒一片。奉之於王。王出所有毀劒一片合之。血出連爲一劍。王謂類利曰。汝實我子。有何神聖乎。類利應聲。擧身聳空。乘牖中日。示其神聖之異。王大悅。立爲太子。)我性本質木。性不喜奇詭。初看東明事。疑幻又疑鬼。徐徐漸相涉。變化難擬議。況是直筆文。一字無虛字。神哉又神哉。萬世之所韙。因思草創君。非聖卽何以。劉媼息大澤。遇神於夢寐。雷電塞晦暝。蛟龍盤怪傀。因之卽有娠。乃生聖劉季。是惟赤帝子。其興多殊祚。世祖始生時。滿室光炳煒。自應赤伏符。掃除黃巾僞。自古帝王興。徵瑞紛蔚蔚。未嗣多怠荒。共絶先王祀。乃知守成君。集蓼戒小毖。守位以寬仁。化民由禮義。永永傳子孫。御國多年紀。

paragraphs.en:
The primal breath divided out of the undifferentiated chaos;
the Heavenly Sovereign and the Earthly Sovereign arose.
Thirteen heads they had, and eleven heads;
their forms and features were full of marvels.
The other sage emperors and kings
are likewise fully recorded in the classics and histories.
Nüjie was stirred by a great star
and bore Dahao Zhi;
Nüshu bore Zhuanxu,
likewise stirred by the radiance of the star Yaoguang.
Fuxi made the sacrificial victims;
Suiren first drilled the fire.
Calendar-plants sprouted: the omen of the Exalted Emperor [Gaodi; identity uncertain];
millet rained down: the auspice of Shennong.
The blue sky Nüwa mended;
the great flood Great Yu set in order.
When the Yellow Emperor was about to ascend to heaven,
a dragon with drooping whiskers came of itself.
In the age of high antiquity, pure and simple,
the numinous sages are hard to record in full.
Later ages gradually grew shallow and thin,
and customs, as a rule, turned extravagant.
Sages are born only now and then,
and divine traces are seldom shown.
In the third year of Shenjue of Han,
in early summer, when the Dipper stood at Si, (In the fourth month of the third year of Shenjue of Han, the jiayin day.)
Hae Mo-su of Haedong [Korea]
was truly a son of Heaven. (The Annals [本記] say: Haeburu, king of Buyeo, was old and had no son. He sacrificed to the mountains and rivers, seeking an heir. The horse he rode came to Gonyeon [Kun Pool]; seeing a great stone, it shed tears. The king thought this strange and had men turn the stone over. There was a small child, golden in colour, shaped like a frog. The king said, "Has Heaven bestowed this fine heir on me?" So he took him in and raised him, and named him Geumwa [Gold Frog], and made him crown prince. His chancellor Aranbul said, "Recently Heaven descended to me and said: 'I will have my descendants found a state here. You must avoid it. By the shore of the Eastern Sea there is a land called Gaseobwon; the soil suits the five grains; it can be made a capital.'" Aranbul urged the king to move the capital, and it was called East Buyeo. In the old capital, Hae Mo-su came as a son of the Heavenly Emperor and made it his capital.)
He first came down out of the sky,
his body riding the track of five dragons;
his followers numbered over a hundred,
riding swans, in a flutter of feathered robes.
Pure music sounded, ringing and swelling;
coloured clouds floated, soft and trailing. (In the third year of Shenjue of Han, the renxu year, the Heavenly Emperor sent his crown prince down to roam the old capital of the king of Buyeo; he was called Hae Mo-su. He came down from Heaven riding a carriage of five dragons; his followers, over a hundred, all rode white swans. Coloured clouds floated above; music resounded within the clouds. He halted at Mount Ungsim; after more than ten days he at last came down. On his head he wore a cap of black feathers; at his waist he wore a sword of dragon-light.)
From of old, rulers who received the Mandate:
which of them was not given by Heaven?
But to descend in broad daylight from the azure heights
had never been seen before.
Mornings he dwelt in the world of men;
evenings he returned within the palace of Heaven. (In the morning he attended to affairs; in the evening he ascended to Heaven. The world called him the Young Lord Heavenly King [天王郞].)
I have heard from the ancients
that the blue vault is distant from the earth by 二億萬八千七百八十 li [the figure as written in the source; an immense distance].
By ladder and plank-road it is hard to climb;
on feathered wings one flies and easily tires.
Yet to rise and descend at will, morning and evening:
by what principle can this be so?
North of the city there is the Green River, (The Green River is today's Amnok River.)
and the River Count had three beautiful daughters (The eldest was called Yuhwa; the next, Hwonhwa; the youngest, Wihwa.)
who parted the waves of the duck-head green
and went to play on the banks of Ungsim. (Coming out of the Green River, they went to play on the Ungsim Pool.)
Their jade pendants chimed in tinkling notes;
their slender faces were charming as flowers. (Their divine bearing was lustrous and beautiful; their assorted pendants tinkled and rang; there was no difference from [the goddesses of] Hangao.)
At first he suspected the shore of Hangao,
then thought of the islet of the Luo River.
The king, out hunting, saw them
and followed them with his eyes, taking much notice.
This was not delight in showy beauty;
truly he was anxious to produce an heir. (The king said to his attendants, "If I could take one as consort, I could have an heir.")
The three daughters, seeing the lord approach,
entered the water to avoid him.
He meant to build a palace,
lying in wait for them to come and play together.
With one stroke of his horsewhip on the ground
a bronze chamber suddenly stood there.
Brocade mats were spread, dazzling bright;
golden goblets were set with rich, fine wine.
Tripping lightly, they indeed walked in of themselves,
and drinking face to face were soon drunk. (The women, seeing the king, at once entered the water. His attendants said, "Great King, why not build a palace, wait for the women to enter the chamber, and block the door against them?" The king thought so too. With his horsewhip he drew on the ground, and a bronze chamber at once stood there, grand and beautiful. In the chamber he set out three seats and placed a cask of wine. The women each sat on their seat, urged one another to drink, and became very drunk, and so on.)
The king then came out and blocked their way;
in alarm they fled, nearly stumbling. (The king waited until the three women were very drunk, then came out in haste and blocked the women; they fled in fright. The eldest, Yuhwa, was stopped by the king.)
The eldest daughter, named Yuhwa [Willow Blossom],
was the one the king stopped.
The River Count was greatly enraged
and sent a messenger, urgent and swift,
to say, "Who are you
that you dare act so lightly and wantonly?"
He replied, "I am the Son of the Heavenly Emperor;
of a lofty clan, I ask to be joined in kinship."
He pointed to the sky, and a dragon chariot descended;
straight he went to the deep sea-palace. (The River Count was greatly enraged and sent an envoy to say, "Who are you, that you detain my daughter?" The king replied, "I am a son of the Heavenly Emperor, and now wish to enter into marriage with the River Count." The River Count again sent word: "If you are a son of the Heavenly Emperor, then when you seek marriage with me you ought to send a matchmaker, and so on. Now you have simply detained my daughter - how discourteous!" The king was ashamed. He was about to go and see the River Count but could not enter the chamber, and wished to release the woman; but the woman had already formed affection for the king and would not leave. So she urged the king: "If you had a dragon carriage, you could reach the River Count's realm." The king pointed to Heaven and announced it; presently a carriage of five dragons came down from the sky. The king and the woman boarded the carriage; wind and clouds suddenly arose, and they reached his palace.)
The River Count then said to the king,
"Marriage is a great matter;
go-betweens and betrothal gifts have established rules.
How can you act on your own whim? (The River Count prepared the ceremony and welcomed him. When they were seated he said, "The way of marriage is the common rule of the world; why have you acted discourteously, shaming my house and lineage? ...", and so on.)
If you are the scion of the Supreme Lord,
let us see you try a divine transformation."
In the rippling green waves
the River Count turned into a carp;
the king at once changed into an otter
and seized it instantly, without waiting a half-step.
Then again it grew two wings
and nimbly turned into a pheasant;
the king in turn became a divine hawk,
striking down, how fierce!
The one became a deer and ran;
the other [lit. "I"] became a dhole and gave chase [趡: sense uncertain].
The River Count knew that he had divine power,
set out wine, and they feasted together in joy.
Waiting until he was drunk, he loaded him into a leather carriage
and placed his daughter beside him at the side-rail, (The side of a carriage is called yi [輢].)
intending him to go with his daughter
up in heaven, riding together with reins raised.
Before the carriage had left the water,
the king sobered, and suddenly started up in alarm. (The River Count's wine: only after seven days does one sober.)
He took the girl's golden hairpin
and pierced the leather, going out through the hole (rhyme-adjusted reading [叶韻]),
and alone ascended the crimson sky;
in silence he did not turn his steed back. (The River Count said, "You are a son of the Heavenly Emperor; what divine marvels do you have?" The king said, "It is only for you to test." Thereupon the River Count, in the water before the courtyard, turned into a carp and swam with the waves. The king turned into an otter and caught it. The River Count again turned into a deer and ran; the king turned into a dhole and chased it. The River Count turned into a pheasant; the king turned into a hawk and struck it. The River Count, believing him truly a son of the Heavenly Emperor, completed the marriage with due ceremony. Fearing that the king had no intention of taking his daughter away with him, he set out music and wine and urged the king to get very drunk; then he put him together with the woman into a small leather carriage and loaded it on the dragon carriage, meaning to make them ascend to Heaven. Before the carriage had left the water, the king sobered up. He took the woman's golden hairpin and pierced the leather carriage, and from the hole alone went out and ascended to Heaven.)
The River Count reproached his daughter,
pulling her lips until they stretched three feet long.
Then he banished her to the Ubal waters
with only two attendants, a maid and a manservant. (The River Count was greatly enraged. [The text reads 其女曰, "his daughter said", but the sense requires that he spoke to his daughter, perhaps with 謂 lost - ?] "You did not follow my instruction; in the end you [欲, "want"; probably an error for 辱, "disgrace" - ?] my house." He had his attendants twist and pull the woman's mouth, so that her lips and mouth became three chi long; with only two servants he banished her into the waters of Ubal. Ubal is the name of a marsh; it is now south of Mount Taebaek.)
A fisherman, watching the waves,
saw a strange beast moving about, dull and awkward,
and reported it to King Geumwa,
who cast an iron net into the gushing water.
They drew up a woman sitting on a rock;
her appearance was fearsome.
Her lips were long and she could not speak;
only after they cut them three times could she open her teeth. (The fisherman Gangnyeok Buchu [強力扶鄒; taken as a personal name, ?] reported: "Recently something has been stealing the fish in the weir and carrying them off; I do not know what beast it is." The king then had the fishermen draw it out with a net; the net tore. He made an iron net and drew it again, and at last they got a woman, who came out seated on a stone. The woman's lips were long and she could not speak; they had her lips cut three times, and then she spoke.)
The king knew her to be Mo-su's consort
and so settled her in a separate palace.
Embracing the sun, she bore Jumong;
that year was the year gye.
His bone structure was truly most extraordinary,
and his cry was also very mighty.
At birth it was an egg as big as a sheng measure;
the onlookers were all startled and shaken.
The king thought it inauspicious:
"Could this be of the human kind?"
He put it in the horse pasture,
and the horses all refused to trample it;
he cast it away in the deep mountains,
and all the beasts gathered round to guard it. (The king knew her to be the consort of a son of the Heavenly Emperor and placed her in a separate palace. Sunlight shone into the woman's bosom, and by this she became pregnant. In the fourth year of Shenjue, the guihai year, in the fourth month of summer, she bore Jumong. His crying was very grand, and his bone structure and bearing were outstanding and rare. At birth, an egg came forth from under his left armpit, as large as about five sheng. The king thought it strange and said, "For a person to give birth to a bird's egg - it may be called inauspicious." He had it placed in the horse pasture; the herds of horses would not trample it. He had it cast away in the deep mountains; all the beasts protected it. On cloudy days there was always sunlight upon the egg. The king took the egg and sent it to the mother to rear. In the end the egg opened and a boy was found. Before a month had passed since his birth, his speech was already 竝實 [all "substantial", perhaps fully articulate - sense uncertain, ?].)
The mother then took it up and nurtured it;
after a month it began to speak.
He said of himself, "Flies bite my eyes;
lying down, I cannot sleep in peace."
His mother made him a bow and arrows,
and his bow never drew in vain. (He said to his mother, "A swarm of flies bites my eyes; I cannot sleep. Mother, make me a bow and arrows." His mother made a bow and arrows of 蓽 [a wicker-like brushwood; the exact plant is uncertain, ?] and gave them to him. He shot at the flies on the spinning wheel himself, and every arrow he loosed hit its mark. Buyeo called a good archer "Jumong.")
As the years went by he grew up,
and his talents became more complete each day.
The crown prince of the king of Buyeo
felt jealousy in his heart
and said, "This Jumong
must be no ordinary man;
if we do not plan against him early,
the trouble will truly never end." (When he had grown up, his talents were fully complete. Geumwa had seven sons, who often went hunting with Jumong. The princes and their followers, more than forty men, caught only one deer, while Jumong shot very many. The princes envied him; they seized Jumong and bound him to a tree, took the deer and left. Jumong pulled up the tree and left. The crown prince Daeso said to the king, "This Jumong is a man of divine valour, and his gaze is extraordinary. If you do not plan against him early, there will surely be trouble later.")
The king ordered him to go and tend the horses,
wishing to test his will.
He thought to himself, "I am Heaven's grandson;
a menial herdsman, truly shameful."
Pressing his hand to his heart, he constantly said in secret,
"My life is no better than death."
He meant to go to the southern lands
and found a state and found a city;
but because his loving mother was alive,
parting was truly not easy. (The king made Jumong tend the horses, wishing to test his intentions. Jumong inwardly harboured resentment and said to his mother, "I am a grandson of the Heavenly Emperor, and I tend horses for another; living is worse than dying. I want to go to the southern land and make a state, but with my mother here I dare not decide for myself." His mother ... and so on.)
His mother, hearing these words,
wiped away clear, flowing tears:
"I beg you, do not be anxious on my account;
I too have always grieved over this.
A gentleman setting out on a long road
must rely on a fine steed."
Together they went to the stable
and struck at once with a long whip;
the horses all bolted,
and one red horse, splendid in colour,
leapt over a fence two zhang high,
and only then did she realise it was a superb steed. (The Tongdian says: What Jumong rode were all "guoxia" [果下; small horses, able to pass under fruit trees].)
Secretly she pricked its tongue with a needle;
sore and aching, it would not take its fodder.
Within days its body grew very thin,
resembling a worn-out nag.
Afterward the king, making his rounds to look,
gave him a horse: it was this very one.
Having got it, he first pulled out the needle,
and day and night often added feed. (His mother said, "This is why my heart rots day and night. I have heard that a gentleman crossing a long road must rely on a swift steed. I can choose horses." She then went to the horse pasture and at once lashed about with a long whip; the herd all bolted in fright, and one reddish horse leapt over a fence two zhang high. Jumong, knowing the horse was swift and outstanding, secretly drove a needle into the root of the horse's tongue. The horse's tongue hurt, and it would not eat water or grass, and grew very thin and haggard. The king toured the horse pasture and, seeing the herd all fat, was greatly pleased; he accordingly granted the lean one to Jumong. Jumong got it, pulled out the needle and fed it extra, it is said.)
Quietly he made friends with three worthy men,
all of whom were wise. (Oi, Mari, Hyeopbo and the like: three men in all.)
Going south, they reached Eomche; (Another name is the Gaesa River. It is north-east of today's Amnok.)
he wished to cross, but there was no boat moored. (Wanting to cross but having no boat, and fearing the pursuing troops would suddenly overtake him, he pointed to Heaven with his whip and sighed with deep feeling, saying, "I am a grandson of the Heavenly Emperor and a 甥 of the River Count [here his daughter's son]. Now, fleeing calamity, I have come to this place. August Heaven and Sovereign Earth, take pity on me, a lone child, and quickly bring me a boat or bridge." When he had finished speaking, he struck the water with his bow; fish and turtles floated up and formed a bridge, and Jumong was able to cross. After a good while the pursuing troops arrived.)
Holding his whip, he pointed to the blue sky
and, with deep feeling, let out a long sigh:
"Grandson of Heaven, kin of the River Count by his daughter,
fleeing peril, he has come to this place.
Pitiful is the heart of a lone son:
can Heaven and Earth bear to abandon him?"
Taking his bow, he struck the river water;
fish and turtles lined up head to tail
and stood firm as a bridge or ladder,
and only then could he cross.
Presently the pursuing soldiers arrived;
when they stepped onto the bridge, it promptly collapsed. (When the pursuing troops reached the river, the bridge of fish and turtles at once vanished; those who had already gone up onto the bridge all sank and died.)
A pair of doves flew holding barley in their beaks,
coming as messengers of the divine mother. (At the parting, Jumong could not bear to be separated. His mother said, "Do not let the thought of one mother weigh on you." She then wrapped seeds of the five grains and sent them with him. Jumong, cut to the heart by the sorrow of a living separation, forgot the barley seeds. Jumong rested beneath a great tree; a pair of doves came and gathered. Jumong said, "Surely these are messengers of my divine mother, sending the barley seeds." He then drew his bow and shot at them; one arrow brought both down. He opened the throat and found the barley seeds. He sprayed the doves with water; they revived and flew off, and so on.)
In a place of superb terrain he opened a royal capital;
mountains and rivers were dense and lofty.
He himself sat upon a makeshift mat of reeds
and roughly settled the ranks of lord and subject. (The king himself sat upon bundled reeds [茀蕝, reeds set up to mark ranks at a court ceremony; sense here uncertain, ?] and roughly fixed the ranks of lord and subject.)
Hah! King Biryu,
how could he not measure himself?
Stubbornly he boasted of descent from an immortal
and did not recognise the nobility of the Emperor's grandson.
He merely wished to make him a vassal,
and the words he spoke were neither prudent nor timid.
He did not hit the navel of the painted deer,
while I, to his astonishment, toppled the jade ring [玉指, the jade-ring episode; wording uncertain]. (Songyang, king of Biryu, was out hunting; seeing the king's extraordinary appearance, he drew him over to sit with him and said, "I live in a remote corner by the sea and have never had the chance to meet a gentleman. Today's chance meeting - how fortunate! Who are you, and where do you come from?" The king said, "I am a grandson of the Heavenly Emperor and king of a western country. May I ask whom you, O King, succeed?" Yang said, "I am a descendant of an immortal; for generations I have been king. Now the land is extremely small and cannot be divided between two kings. You have founded your state only recently; would it be acceptable to be my dependency?" The king said, "I succeed Heaven. Now you are not a descendant of a god, yet you forcibly style yourself king. If you do not submit to me, Heaven will surely strike you down." Songyang, since the king repeatedly called himself a grandson of Heaven, inwardly doubted him and wished to test his ability; so he said, "I wish to shoot with you." They set a painted deer within a hundred paces and shot at it. His arrow [Songyang's, ?] did not enter the deer's navel, as if his hand were upside-down [?]. The king had a man hang a jade finger-ring beyond a hundred paces and shot at it; it broke apart like shattered tile. Songyang was greatly astonished, and so on.)
He came to see how the drum and horn had changed,
and dared not claim them as his instruments; (The king said, "Because the work of the state is newly established, I do not yet have drums and horns and ceremonial dignity. When Biryu's envoys come and go, I cannot greet and see them off with the rites due a king. That is why they slight me." His retainer Bubunno came forward and said, "Your servant will fetch Biryu's drums and horns for the Great King." The king said, "They are another state's stored things; why should you take them?" He replied, "These are things Heaven has given. Why not take them? When the Great King was hard-pressed in Buyeo, who would have said that the Great King could come to this? Now the Great King, rousing himself from the peril of ten thousand deaths, has made his name known in Liaozuo [east of the Liao]. This is done by the command of the Heavenly Emperor; what could fail?" Thereupon Bubunno and others, three men in all, went to Biryu and took the drums and came back. The king of Biryu sent an envoy to say ..., and so on. The king, fearing that [Biryu] would come to look at the drums and horns, [had] their colour darkened as if old [the verb is lacking in the text, ?]. Songyang did not dare to dispute it and left.)
he came to see that the pillars of the house were old,
and clicked his tongue, ashamed in turn. (Songyang wished to settle it by the order in which their capitals had been founded, the earlier or the later [of the two] becoming the vassal [text 先後爲附庸; the construction is unclear, ?]. The king built palaces, using rotten wood for the pillars, so that they seemed a thousand years old. Songyang came and saw them, and in the end did not dare to dispute the precedence in founding the capital.)
When Dongmyeong hunted in the west,
he happened to catch a snow-white deer (a large deer is called gwe [麂])
and hung it upside down on Crab Plain,
and dared to utter a curse and say,
"If Heaven does not rain on Biryu,
drowning and sinking its capital and countryside,
I will surely not let you go;
you must help my wrath."
The deer's cry was most piteous,
and reached up to Heaven's ears.
Unceasing rain poured for seven days,
abundant as if the Huai and the Si had been overturned.
Songyang was greatly anxious and afraid;
along the stream he vainly stretched reeds across.
The people vied to come and cling to them,
sweat streaming, staring at one another.
Dongmyeong then took his whip
and drew on the water, and the surging water stopped.
Songyang surrendered with his whole country;
after this none dared slander me. (Hunting in the west, he caught a white deer. He hung it upside down at Crab Plain and cursed, saying, "If Heaven does not send rain to wash away and submerge the capital of the king of Biryu, I surely will not let you go. If you wish to escape this ordeal, you must appeal to Heaven." The deer cried piteously, and the sound reached Heaven. Continuous rain fell for seven days and swept away and submerged Songyang's capital. The king laid a reed rope across the current and rode a "duck-horse" [鴨馬; sense uncertain, ?]; the people all held the rope. Jumong drew a line on the water with his whip, and the water at once subsided. In the sixth month Songyang came and submitted with his whole state, and so on.)
Dark clouds veiled Falcon Ridge,
and the winding mountains were not seen.
There were several thousand people,
and the sound of chopping wood was faintly heard.
The king said, "Heaven is building a city for me
at its foot."
Suddenly the clouds and mist dispersed,
and palace towers rose high and towering. (In the seventh month, dark clouds rose over Gol Ridge [鶻嶺]. People could not see the mountain; they only heard the voices of several thousand people carrying out earthworks. The king said, "Heaven is building a city for me." After seven days the clouds and mist dispersed of themselves, and the walls, palaces and terraces had come into being by themselves. The king bowed to August Heaven and took up residence.)
He reigned nineteen years,
ascended to heaven and did not descend to rule. (In autumn, the ninth month, the king ascended to Heaven and did not come down; he was forty years old at the time. The crown prince buried the jade whip he had left behind at Mount Yong [龍山], and so on.)
Magnificent, he had extraordinary integrity.
His eldest son was called Yuri;
having obtained the sword, he succeeded to his father's throne.
He plugged the basin to stop a person's scolding. (Yuri in his youth had extraordinary spirit, and so on. In youth he made his living shooting sparrows with pellets. He saw a woman carrying a water jar on her head and shot it to pieces. The woman angrily scolded him: "A child without a father! He has shot my jar to pieces!" Yuri was greatly ashamed. He shot clay pellets at the jar and plugged the hole as before. He went home and asked his mother, "Who is my father?" His mother, because Yuri was young, said to him teasingly, "You have no fixed father." Yuri wept and said, "A person without a fixed father - with what face can I see others?" He was about to cut his own throat. His mother, greatly startled, stopped him, saying, "My earlier words were only a joke. Your father is a grandson of the Heavenly Emperor and a 甥 of the River Count [i.e. his daughter's son]. Resenting being a subject of Buyeo, he fled to the southern land and first founded a state. Will you go and see him?" He answered, "The father is a ruler of men and the son a subject; though I am untalented, would I not be ashamed?" His mother said, "When your father left, he left a word: 'I have a hidden object: the pine on the stone, at seven ridges and seven valleys. One who can get this is my son.'" Yuri went to the mountains and valleys himself, searched without finding it, and returned exhausted. Yuri heard a sad sound from the pillar of the hall. That pillar was in fact the pine wood on the stone; its body had seven edges. Yuri worked it out himself, saying, "'Seven ridges and seven valleys' means seven edges; 'the pine on the stone' means the pillar." He rose and went to look at it: there was a hole in the pillar, and he found a piece of broken sword and was overjoyed. In the fourth year of Hongjia of Former Han, in the fourth month of summer, he fled to Goguryeo. He presented the piece of sword to the king. The king took out the piece of broken sword that he had and joined them; blood came out and they joined into one sword. The king said to Yuri, "You are truly my son. What divine sanctity do you have?" Yuri at once, in answer, lifted his body and soared into the air, riding the sunlight in the window [i.e. perhaps a sunbeam through the window - ?], to show the marvel of his divine sanctity. The king was greatly delighted and made him crown prince.)
By nature I am plain and rustic;
by temperament I do not like the strange and bizarre.
When I first read the Dongmyeong story,
I suspected illusion and suspected ghosts.
Slowly, gradually, I waded into it:
its transformations were hard to conjecture or discuss.
Moreover it is a text of straight brush,
without a single empty character.
How divine, and again how divine!
Affirmed through ten thousand generations.
So I reflect on the founding rulers:
if they were not sages, what were they?
Old Mother Liu rested by the great marsh
and met a spirit in her dream;
thunder and lightning filled the darkness,
and a flood-dragon coiled, strange and monstrous.
Thereupon she conceived
and bore the sage Liu Ji [Liu Bang].
He was the Son of the Red Emperor;
his rise was attended by many extraordinary blessings.
When Shizu [Emperor Guangwu] was first born,
the room was filled with blazing light.
He himself answered the Chifu ("Red Fu") talisman
and swept away the Yellow Turban impostors.
From of old, when emperors and kings arose,
omens and auspicious signs were abundant and lush.
Their heirs were mostly idle and dissolute,
and together cut off the sacrifices to the former kings.
Thus I know that rulers who preserve what has been achieved
heed "gathering on the smartweed" and "be cautious of small troubles,"
guard their position with generosity and benevolence,
transform the people through ritual and righteousness,
and hand it down to their descendants for ever and ever,
ruling the country for many years.
